runaway-slave.hook: Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh, a Companion whom the Prophet never turned away and always met with a smile ([Bukhārī 3822](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3822)), reports three sayings about a slave who flees his master: his prayer is not accepted, the protection owed him lapses, and he has committed an act of unbelief (kufr) until he returns. Bukhārī 5286, from Ibn ʿAbbās, records that slaves who fled hostile pagans to the Muslims were counted free.
runaway-slave.takeaway: In Muslim 70 the Prophet says a runaway slave's prayer ‘is not accepted’; Muslim 68 calls the flight ‘an act of infidelity as long as he would not return to him’.

showcase.note: In Muslim 68 a later narrator in the chain adds “this hadith was narrated from the Apostle”. Muslim 69 and 70 give the words as the Prophet's.

items.label: Muslim 70 · the Prophet's words
items.text: When the slave runs away from his master, his prayer is not accepted

items.label: Muslim 69 · the Prophet's words
items.text: The slave who fled from his master, responsibility with regard to him was absolved

items.label: Muslim 68 · Jarīr's words
items.text: The slave who fled from his master committed an act of infidelity as long as he would not return to him.

keyQuote.text: When the slave runs away from his master, his prayer is not accepted

classical.text: Al-Nawawī gives four readings of kufr in such sayings: the soundest, that it is a deed of the unbelievers and the ways of the pre-Islamic age (Jāhiliyya); or that it leads to unbelief; or ingratitude for a favour; or that it applies to one who holds running away lawful. Al-Māzarī, a Mālikī jurist who wrote a commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, and al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ read the unaccepted prayer the last way, as said of a slave who holds running away lawful; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, author of the classic handbook of the science of hadith, rejected that and held that it applies to any runaway, whose prayer is valid but brings no reward, and al-Nawawī agrees. On the protection that lapses, he quotes Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ again: a slave was protected from his master's punishment and confinement, and that protection lapses when he runs away. He explains that Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, a narrator of Kūfa whom the critics called precise and reliable, who narrated Muslim 68 as Jarīr's words, did not want to name the Prophet as its source in Basra, where the Khārijites, an early sect that broke with ʿAlī, held to its plain sense.

runaway-slave.comparison:
Each reading of these sayings needs something their words do not state. The reading of al-Māzarī and ʿIyāḍ needs a condition, that the slave holds running away lawful, which the sayings do not mention; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ rejected it, and al-Nawawī agreed. The figurative readings of kufr rest on how other sayings use the word, as when fighting a Muslim is called kufr ([Bukhārī 48](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:48)).

The witness is Jarīr; in Muslim 68 the narrator Manṣūr swears that it comes from the Prophet.

Either the warnings concern a slave who holds flight lawful, a condition the words do not carry; or they concern every runaway, as Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and al-Nawawī hold, and then each runaway's prayer brings no reward and his protection from his master's punishment lapses until he goes back. Bukhārī 5286 records another rule for slaves of hostile pagans who reached the Muslims: they “would be considered free persons (not slaves)”. For a slave who flees his master, the warning sets no end but his return: “The slave who fled from his master committed an act of infidelity as long as he would not return to him” ([Muslim 68](https://sunnah.com/muslim:68)).

walad-lil-firash.title: One Case in 6 Reports: A Slave-Woman's Son Assigned to Her Owner's Line Despite His Likeness to Another Man
walad-lil-firash.context: Bukhārī and Muslim, from ʿĀʾishah, at the conquest of Mecca: two men claim the son of Zamʿa's slave-woman.
walad-lil-firash.hook: Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ claimed a boy as his brother ʿUtba's son; ʿAbd ibn Zamʿa claimed him as his own brother, born to his father's slave-woman. The Prophet saw the likeness to ʿUtba, ruled for ʿAbd, and told Sawda, the Prophet's wife and ʿAbd's sister (whom the ruling made the boy's sister), to screen herself from the boy.
walad-lil-firash.takeaway: The Prophet ruled the son of Zamʿa's slave-woman to be ʿAbd ibn Zamʿa's brother because ‘the boy is for the owner of the bed’, though he saw a resemblance to ʿUtba (Bukhārī 6765).

showcase.note: To his wife Sawda: “Screen yourself from this boy”; “Since then the boy did not see Sauda till he died” (Bukhārī 2745).

items.text: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) looked at his resemblance and found a clear resemblance with 'Utba.
the boy is for the owner of the bed, and the stone is for the adulterer

keyQuote.text: This boy is for you as the boy belongs to the bed (where he was born), and for the adulterer is the stone (i.e. deprivation).

classical.text: Ibn Ḥajar explains the “bed” (firāsh), the marriage or ownership that makes a child legally the husband's or owner's: a slave-woman becomes her owner's bed through intercourse, and if the owner acknowledges it, a child she bears within the possible term is attributed to him. A wife becomes the bed by the marriage contract alone, he notes, because a slave-woman is acquired for other purposes too. On the order to Sawda to veil herself from the boy, he records three explanations: precaution against doubt (a commentator he cites, and the Shāfiʿī school, which takes the order as a recommendation); a stricter veil for the Prophet's wives; and, in the Mālikī school, a ruling between two rulings, in which the bed decides lineage and the clear likeness decides the veil.

walad-lil-firash.comparison:
Each explanation of the veil needs the Prophet to have kept the likeness in view after ruling by the bed. The reports say so themselves: he gave the order when he saw the boy's resemblance to ʿUtba (Bukhārī 2745, 6765; Muslim 1457a).

The witness is ʿĀʾishah, Sawda's fellow wife, from whom al-Dhahabī counts 2,210 hadith ([Siyar 2/139](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/143/)); Bukhārī carries this case in five places.

Either the boy was Zamʿa's son, as the ruling declared, and his sister was told to veil herself from her brother; or he was ʿUtba's, as the likeness suggested, and the ruling gave him a lineage through his mother's owner. On both, the ruling rests on what Ibn Ḥajar describes: the owner's relations with his slave-woman made her his bed. The report ends on the veil: “Since then the boy did not see Sauda till he died” ([Bukhārī 2745](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2745)).

booty-share.title: Women and Slaves Who Join a Battle Get ‘a Prize’, Not a Fixed Share: Ibn ʿAbbās Answers a Letter
booty-share.context: Muslim 1812: Ibn ʿAbbās's written replies to Najda, a Khārijite (Muslim calls him al-Ḥarūrī, the name the reports give the Khārijites), on shares of the booty.
booty-share.hook: Asked in a letter whether women and slaves who fight receive a share of the booty, Ibn ʿAbbās answers that they receive a prize or some reward, with no fixed share. These are his answers, not words of the Prophet, and one of the three reports concerns women and does not mention slaves.
booty-share.takeaway: Ibn ʿAbbās writes that women and slaves who join a battle have ‘no fixed share’ of the booty and ‘will be given some reward from the spoils of war’ (Muslim 1812e).

showcase.note: These are Ibn ʿAbbās's written answers; 1812a describes the Prophet's practice with women.

items.label: Muslim 1812c
items.text: You have written asking about the woman and the slave whether they would get a share of the booty if they participated in Jihad. (You should know that) there is nothing of the sort for them except that they will be given a prize.

items.label: Muslim 1812e
items.text: And you have inquired whether there is a fixed share of the booty for women and slaves when they participate in a battle. (I have to tell you that) there is no fixed share for them except that they will be given some reward from the spoils of war

items.label: Muslim 1812a · about women, not slaves
items.text: They would treat the wounded and were given a reward from the booty, but he did not assign any regular share for them.

keyQuote.text: And you have inquired whether there is a fixed share of the booty for women and slaves when they participate in a battle. (I have to tell you that) there is no fixed share for them except that they will be given some reward from the spoils of war

booty-share.comparison: These are Ibn ʿAbbās's answers, not words of the Prophet, and Muslim 1812a describes the Prophet's practice with women: “he did not assign any regular share for them”. Ibn ʿAbbās puts the slave beside the woman under the same rule: “there is nothing of the sort for them except that they will be given a prize” (Muslim 1812c).

ransom-returned.title: One Case in 7 Texts: ‘As for Your Sheep and Slave Girl, They Are to Be Returned to You’
ransom-returned.context: Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayra and Zayd ibn Khālid: a father who paid a ransom over his son's adultery asks the Prophet to judge.
ransom-returned.hook: A father told the Prophet that his son, a hired labourer, had committed adultery with his employer's wife, and that he had paid a ransom of a hundred sheep and a slave girl. The Prophet voided the payment, returned the sheep and the slave girl to him, and applied the prescribed punishments.
ransom-returned.takeaway: In Bukhārī 6633 the Prophet voids a ransom of ‘one-hundred sheep and a slave girl’ paid in an adultery case and returns both to the father.

showcase.note: 7 texts under 13 numbers (6 Sunnah.com combined entries).

points.text: I ransomed him with one-hundred sheep and a slave girl.
I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws: As for your sheep and slave girl, they are to be returned to you.
Then he scourged his son one hundred lashes and exiled him for one year.

keyQuote.text: As for your sheep and slave girl, they are to be returned to you.

ransom-returned.comparison: The ruling's point is that a prescribed punishment cannot be bought off, and the Prophet swore to judge by God's law. The slave girl appears inside that ruling as part of the price, listed with the sheep and returned with them to the man who owned her: “As for your sheep and slave girl, they are to be returned to you” (Bukhārī 6633).

where-is-allah.title: ‘Where Is Allah?’: The Prophet Questions a Slave Woman, Then Says ‘Grant Her Freedom, She Is a Believing Woman’
where-is-allah.context: Muslim 537a: a man who slapped his shepherd slave-woman asks the Prophet whether he should free her.
where-is-allah.hook: Muʿāwiya ibn al-Ḥakam, a Companion who prayed behind the Prophet ([Muslim 537a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:537a)), not the later caliph Muʿāwiya, slapped the slave-woman who tended his goats after a wolf took one, and came to the Prophet troubled by it. He asked whether he should free her; the Prophet asked her two questions and said, ‘Grant her freedom, she is a believing woman’.
where-is-allah.takeaway: In Muslim 537a the Prophet treats Muʿāwiya's slap as grave, questions his slave-woman, and tells him, ‘Grant her freedom, she is a believing woman’.

showcase.note: Arabic: fa-ʿaẓẓama dhālika ʿalayya, he (the Prophet) made it a grave matter for me; Sunnah.com's English leaves open who felt it grievous.

points.text: So I slapped her. I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and felt (this act of mine) as something grievous
Messenger of Allah, should I not grant her freedom? He (the Holy Prophet) said: Bring her to me.
He said to her: Where is Allah? She said: He is in the heaven. He said: Who am I? She said: Thou art the Messenger of Allah.
He said: Grant her freedom, she is a believing woman

keyQuote.text: He said: Grant her freedom, she is a believing woman

classical.text: Al-Nawawī reads the questions as a test of whether she was a monotheist or an idol-worshipper; when she said “in the heaven”, he knew she was a monotheist. He draws from the report that freeing a believer is better than freeing an unbeliever, and notes that scholars agree an unbeliever may be freed outside the expiations (kaffāra); for the expiations, al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and the majority accept a believing slave and no other, while Abū Ḥanīfa accepted any.

where-is-allah.comparison:
Al-Nawawī's reading needs the questions to have been a test of her faith, and the report bears it out: the Prophet asks two questions and gives her answer as his reason. From it he draws that freeing a believer is better than freeing an unbeliever, and he notes that for most expiations al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and the majority accept a believing slave and no other.

The witness is Muʿāwiya ibn al-Ḥakam al-Sulamī, the man who struck her; the account is his own.

The freeing was Muʿāwiya's offer, made after the Prophet treated the slap as grave. Either it was a voluntary freeing, which scholars agree may be given to an unbeliever, and the Prophet still asked about her faith first; or it served as an expiation, for which the majority required a believer, and her freedom depended on her answers. On both, the reason he gave was her faith: “Grant her freedom, she is a believing woman” ([Muslim 537a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:537a)).

kaffara.title: 5 Reports: ‘Can You Find a Slave to Set Him Free?’, the First Expiation for Breaking the Ramaḍān Fast
kaffara.context: Bukhārī and Muslim, from Abū Hurayra: a man who had intercourse with his wife while fasting in Ramaḍān asks what he must do.
kaffara.hook: Five reports give the expiation for intercourse during the Ramaḍān fast: free a slave; if not, fast two months in a row; if not, feed sixty poor people. The man could do none of these, and the Prophet gave him dates to give away, then let him take them home.
kaffara.takeaway: In Bukhārī 5368 and Muslim 1111a the first expiation for breaking the Ramaḍān fast by intercourse is to free a slave, then two months of fasting, then feeding sixty poor people.

showcase.note: All five reports concern this one expiation. The Qurʾān's expiations for manslaughter, for declaring one's wife to be like one's mother (ẓihār), and for broken oaths (4:92, 58:3, 5:89) are on the Qurʾān page.

points.text: Can you find a slave to set him free?
Can you observe fast for two consecutive months?
Can you provide food to sixty poor people?
Go and give it to your family to eat

keyQuote.text: Manumit a slave (as expiation).

classical.text: Al-Nawawī notes that for the expiations of ẓihār, oaths and intercourse in Ramaḍān, al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and the majority accept a believing slave and no other, while Abū Ḥanīfa and the jurists of Kūfa accepted an unbelieving one as well.

kaffara.comparison:
The Muslim reading of expiations as a path to freedom needs slaves to be at hand to free. The reports assume it: the first question is whether the man can find one, and the fasting and feeding come after it. Al-Nawawī adds that al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and the majority accept a believing slave and no other for this expiation.

The witness is again Abū Hurayra.

Either the expiation is read as a means of reducing slavery, and it works through a slave the man must first find and pay for; or as a penalty on the man, and a slave is its first form of payment. The man's first reply is “I cannot afford that” (Bukhārī 5368). On both readings, the ruling takes for granted that slaves were there to be bought: “Can you find a slave to set him free?” ([Muslim 1111a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1111a)).

master-duties.title: 6 Reports on Owners and Their Slaves: Earnings, Reward, Duty and False Accusation
master-duties.context: Bukhārī: sayings about slaves and their owners, from Abū Hurayra; Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, whom the Prophet sent to govern part of Yemen ([Bukhārī 4341](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4341)); Ibn ʿUmar; and another Companion, ʿAbdallāh ibn Zamʿa.
master-duties.hook: Six sayings in Bukhārī concern the earnings of slave-women, a double reward for freeing and marrying one, a slave as guardian of his master's property, an owner who falsely accuses his slave, and a husband who lashes his wife ‘like a slave’. One line usually quoted with them is Abū Hurayra's own.
master-duties.takeaway: Bukhārī records the Prophet forbidding the earnings of slave-women (5348), warning an owner who slanders his slave of a flogging on the Day of Resurrection (6858), and comparing the lashing of a wife to that of a slave (4942); the upkeep line in 5355 is Abū Hurayra's own.

showcase.note: Bukhārī 5348: “by prostitution” is the translator's gloss; the Arabic reads the earnings of slave-women (kasb al-imāʾ).

items.text: The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade taking the earnings of a slave girl by prostitution
any man who has a slave girl whom he educates properly, teaches good manners, manumits and marries her, will get a double reward
a slave is a guardian of his master's property and is responsible (for that)
If somebody slanders his slave and the slave is free from what he says, he will be flogged on the Day of Resurrection
It is not wise for anyone of you to lash his wife like a slave, for he might sleep with her the same evening.
Abū Hurayra, asked whether the sayings after the Prophet's words (“A slave says, 'Give me food and enjoy my service.'”) were from the Prophet: “No, it is from my own self.”

keyQuote.text: If somebody slanders his slave and the slave is free from what he says, he will be flogged on the Day of Resurrection unless the slave is really as he has described him

master-duties.comparison: Several of these sayings protect slaves: an owner who slanders his slave is answerable on the Day of Resurrection, and a man who educates, frees and marries his slave-woman earns a double reward. The same sayings take for granted that a slave held his master's property in trust and could be lashed: “It is not wise for anyone of you to lash his wife like a slave” (Bukhārī 4942).

barira.title: One Story in 33 Reports: Barīra Is Bought, Freed, and Chooses to Leave Her Husband
barira.context: Bukhārī and Muslim, mostly from ʿĀʾishah: the story of Barīra, a slave woman who bought her freedom by contract with ʿĀʾishah's help and became ʿĀʾishah's freed slave.
barira.hook: Thirty-three reports tell how Barīra's freedom was bought. She had contracted with her owners to buy it and asked ʿĀʾishah for help; the owners would not sell unless they kept the lasting tie, with a right of inheritance, between a freed slave and the one who freed him (walāʾ); the Prophet told ʿĀʾishah to buy her and voided the condition from the pulpit. Once free, Barīra left her husband and declined the Prophet's request to go back to him.
barira.takeaway: ʿĀʾishah bought and freed Barīra, the Prophet ruled that ‘the wala is for the one who manumits’, and once free Barīra ‘was given the option to keep her husband or leave him’ (Bukhārī 5279).

showcase.note: “for the manumitted” renders li-man aʿtaqa, the one who frees. 33 reports in all (30 on the contract, walāʾ, and marriage choice, plus 3 on meat given to Barīra in charity: Muslim 1074a, 1075a, 1075b), alongside two general sayings on walāʾ (Bukhārī 6756, 6760).

points.text: Barira came to seek her help in writing of emancipation and she had to pay five Uqiya (of gold) by five yearly installments.
They said that they would not agree to it unless her Wala' would be for them.
Buy Barirah and let them stipulate that her Wala' will be for them, as the Wala' is for the manumitted.
Any condition which is not in Allah's Laws is invalid even if there were a hundred such conditions.
When she was manumitted, she was given the option to keep her husband or leave him
He said: “No, I only intercede for him.” She said: “I am not in need of him.”

keyQuote.text: The wala is for the one who manumits

classical.text: Al-Nawawī notes that the instruction to let the sellers stipulate the walāʾ troubled scholars, so much that some rejected the whole hadith, a view reported from Yaḥyā ibn Aktham, a chief judge of the ʿAbbāsid era; the majority accepted it and explained it. Ibn Ḥajar identifies the line “if he were free he would not have given her the option” as the comment of ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, ʿĀʾishah's nephew, who studied under her, not part of the hadith, and the reports differ on whether her husband was slave or free.

barira.comparison:
The scholars' difficulty is the Prophet's instruction to let the sellers stipulate the walāʾ for themselves, “let them stipulate that her Wala' will be for them” (Bukhārī 2729), a condition he then declared void. Each reading needs something the reports do not state. Reading *lahum*, for them, as *ʿalayhim*, against them, needs a sense al-Nawawī calls weak, since the Prophet objected to the condition. His preferred reading, that the permission was particular to this case and given so that voiding it would deter more strongly, needs an intention no report records; he supports it by analogy with the pilgrims told to turn their Ḥajj into ʿUmra. Yaḥyā ibn Aktham rejected the whole hadith.

The witness is ʿĀʾishah, the buyer herself.

Muslims read the story as one of freedom and choice, and the reports bear that out: once free, Barīra left her husband and turned down the Prophet's intercession. Either the sellers were told they could keep a condition that was then voided, as the plain words say; or the words mean something else, by a sense al-Nawawī calls weak or an intention no report states. On every reading her freedom came by sale, her owners bargained over who would inherit from her, and the Prophet settled it for the buyer: “Buy Barira and manumit her and the Wala' will be for the liberator” ([Bukhārī 2560](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2560)).
